sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Svarog** ​(*svarog*) — ‌Sky, ‌Fire, Smithing ​· Bright, ​clear ​— belongs ​to ​the Slavic ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Sky, Fire, ​Smithing". ‌The name ​means ​"Bright, clear"[^1].

​**Svarog** is ​the ​elusive Slavic ‌god ​of the ‌**sky, ​fire, and ‌smithing** — ​known ‌almost entirely ​from ‌a handful ​of early ​Russian ‌and Western ‌chronicle ‌notices that ​name him, ​compare ‌him to ​a ​smith, and ‌make him ​father ​of the ‌sun. ​He is ‌the ​Slavs' heaven-forge: ​the god ​at ​whose anvil ‌the ‌daylight was ​made.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records ​the canonical ​scholarly ‌spelling **Svarog** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ​[its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/svarog/). The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*svarog* contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Svarog** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "Bright, ​clear"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Svarog** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *svarog* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**s** ​→ **S** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **v** ​→ ​**v** — ​Same
- ‌**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**r** → ​**r** ‌— ‌Same
- **o** ​→ ​**o** ​— Same
- ​**g** ‌→ ‌**g** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/svarog/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**svarog** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Svarog.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Svarog" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Svarog" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"svarog" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Svarog ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Svarog ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Svarog ‌place ​sky, fire, ​smithing ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Svarog ‌appears ​in slavic ‌tradition ​as ​sky, fire, ​smithing. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Bright, ​clear", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Svarog ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Svarog ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Svarog ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Svarog ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Svarog, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​sky ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Svarog ​asks what ‌can be ‌known of ​a god ​who ​left almost ​nothing. The ​honest answer ‌is: ​a name, ​a son, ‌a forge, ​and a ‌fire. ​Yet these ‌fragments sketch ​a complete ​theology of ​making. ​The Slavs ​looked at ‌daylight and ​did ‌not call ​it a ‌lamp or ​a face ‌— ​they called ‌it **work**: ​something hammered ​out ‌on an ‌anvil by ‌a craftsman ​whose son ​delivers ‌it. In ​that intuition ​lies a ‌whole philosophy ​— ​that order ‌is manufactured, ​that radiance ‌is ​skilled labor, ​that the ​sky is ​a workshop ‌and ‌the sun ​its product. ‌The hearth-name ​Svarožič extends ​the ‌philosophy downward: ‌if the ‌sun is ‌a ​forge's output, ‌every kitchen ​fire is ​a franchise ​of ‌heaven. A ​civilization that ​imagined the ​cosmos ‌this way ​honored the ​smith as ​its most ‌theologically ​precise citizen. ‌Svarog survives ​because the ‌intuition survives: ​we ‌still speak ‌of 'forging' ​the future, ​still ​feel that ​making is ‌the most ‌godlike of ​acts.[^1]
